item.title: Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
item.description:
Partner content

Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space

September 30, 2026

Dutch homes are famously charming – and famously awkward to furnish – for cabinetmakers at Cabinetheroes, that is the whole point. Narrow facades, steep staircases, and rooms that seem to defy right angles: these aren’t quirks, they’re history.

Property taxes in many Dutch cities were once linked to the width of a building’s frontage, and the result can still be seen today: narrow hallways, steep staircases and rooms where standard furniture is difficult to place.

The familiar hooks above many gabled windows are another reminder of these challenging layouts – they were traditionally used to hoist furniture through the windows because getting large pieces up the stairs was often impossible.

Converted attics bring their own challenges. In a typical “zolder”, sloped ceilings and unusual angles can leave large parts of the room unused. Standard wardrobes are made for straight walls and predictable dimensions, and simply can’t use that kind of space. A made-to-measure cabinet, by contrast, can follow the exact shape of the room and turn overlooked corners into valuable storage. The result: rooms that look bigger on paper than they feel in practice, with corners and slopes often written off as wasted.

“You often have more space than you think – you just aren’t using it yet,” says Sven, managing director of the Cabinetheroes franchise network and an experienced carpenter himself.

Planning around the room, not against it
This is where made-to-measure solutions like those from Cabinetheroes come in. With the Cabinetheroes, creating a cabinet built around a room rather than the other way around is straightforward. Instead of adapting a home to fit off-the-shelf furniture, a personal Cabinethero visits, discusses your ideas, measures the room and plans a solution around the space and the way you live.

As an experienced cabinetmaker, he understands both the design and the craftsmanship behind it, and once the cabinet has been individually manufactured, he also takes care of the professional installation. From the first measurements to the finished cabinet, you have one personal point of contact – and every important step is handled by a skilled professional. Two recent projects show us what this all means in practice.

The hallway that finally feels welcoming
Christian’s hallway was more of a narrow passage than an inviting entrance. A conventional cabinet would have made the space feel even tighter, yet leaving it empty meant coats, shoes and everyday items had nowhere to go.

After measuring the hallway personally, Sven planned a fitted cloakroom cabinet that uses the available space down to the millimetre, with an integrated LED strip adding light and a warmer atmosphere.

“Tidy, I’d say,” is how Christian describes the practical result. But the emotional difference mattered just as much: “You feel welcome.” His verdict on the process was equally clear: “It was really professional. I’d recommend it to anyone.” Every step along the way was handled by one point of contact.

An open dressing area beneath a sloped roof
For Jennifer, a sloped ceiling appeared to rule out a spacious dressing area. Standard wardrobes would have left gaps beneath the roof and wasted valuable space in the lowest parts of the room. The made-to-measure design follows the ceiling precisely and uses the space right into the furthest corner.

Instead of doors, the open layout keeps clothing and accessories visible and easy to reach, with socks, belts and other smaller items each getting their own place, helping the room stay organised in everyday life.

“We’d never had such a beautiful cabinet,” Jennifer says. Everything was “matched exactly to the room”, while the personal planning took place comfortably in her own home. Her conclusion: “Quality, style and something completely individual.”

Starting with the room, not the shop
The lesson from both projects: start with the room rather than with the limited dimensions offered by a furniture shop. Slopes, alcoves and awkward corners are not necessarily wasted space – they simply require accurate measurements and thoughtful planning, with lighting, sockets and everyday routines considered from the beginning.

Features such as integrated LEDs are much easier to incorporate during planning than to add afterwards, and even a few centimetres can determine whether standard furniture fits at all.

As Sven puts it: “Your room can do more.”

For anyone facing a similar layout, the Cabinetheroes offer a free, non-binding enquiry: a personal Cabinethero will visit, discuss the possibilities, take precise measurements and guide the process through to individual planning and professional installation.

item.title: Amsterdam urges health minister to rescue crack treatment study
item.description:
Amsterdam urges health minister to rescue crack treatment study

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The mayor of Amsterdam, Femke Halsema, has called on the government to step in to save an experimental programme to treat crack addicts with a medicine usually prescribed for ADHD.

The inspectorate IGJ has halted production of the medicine, dexamphetamine, at a Dutch hospital as part of an ongoing supervisory procedure.

The IGJ did not name the hospital or say how long the investigation would take, but a spokesman told Dutch News: “We are concerned about the quality of the medicine.”

Amsterdam city council said last week it wanted to start giving the dexamphetamine to people addicted to crack cocaine in an experiment similar to the methadone programme for heroin users.

The probe has been backed by the other three major Dutch cities – Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – after initial research showed it could help ease crack users’ cravings.

Halsema and Alexander Scholtes, alderman responsible for healthcare, said suspending production of the drug would have a devastating impact.

Promising method

They have written to health minister Sophie Hermans urging her to review the IGJ’s decision and come up with a solution to ensure the study can continue.

“What it means is that the only highly promising method for treating these seriously addicted people has gone out of the window,” Scholtes told TV station AT5. “We can’t let that happen.”

The city council said the suspension of production was “unexpected and for reasons that are unclear to us”, but the IGJ said its investigation pre-dated the experimental programme.

They asked Hermans to organise a meeting with all parties concerned before November 1 to discuss a solution. “We value the independent position of the IGJ highly and are not impinging on their judgment,” they wrote.

But they added: “Every day we see people in Amsterdam whose lives are being taken over by a serious crack addiction.”

Amsterdam’s local healthcare authority (GGD) estimates there are between 3,000 and 9,000 crack users in the city, many of whom are homeless or have mental health problems, or both.

The Trimbos institute, which specialises in mental health, and addiction support service Mainline said in a report three years ago that there were around 27,900 problematic crack users in the Netherlands.

item.title: Most major Dutch data centres keep energy usage secret: report
item.description:
Most major Dutch data centres keep energy usage secret: report

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Most data centres in the Netherlands do not make their environmental impact public, which conceals water and electricity usage, according to an investigation by Trouw and Lighthouse Reports.

The Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), which collects data on behalf of the EU, lists only 104 data centres but the industry body Dutch Datacenter Association (DDA) says there were 186 commercial data centres at the end of 2025.

These figures cover data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT capacity, which are required to report their energy and water use, among other things, under the EU’s Energy Efficiency Directive.

The RVO’s list is missing almost half the centres counted by the DDA, and that count does not include the many data centres run in-house by banks, hospitals and other companies. Trouw estimates that public data is available for only around a quarter of large data centres.

Dutch data centre energy 
Data centres used 5.1 billion kWh of electricity in 2024, or 4.6% of the national total, according to statistics from CBS – a 37% rise on 2021. Figures for 2025 are not yet available.

RVO figures published this summer showed that Microsoft’s largest Dutch data centre alone uses 1% of national electricity, though the power is said to come from renewable sources. Google, which runs two large data centres in the Netherlands, does not publish its figures.

Grid operator TenneT expects data centres to account for 10% to 15% of Dutch electricity use by 2030. Water use is lower, at an estimated 0.1% of the national total.

Aarhus Convention 
Reporters working with Lighthouse Reports spent a year filing freedom of information requests in all 27 EU member states and with the European Commission. Most were refused, with some countries saying they did not have the data, and others citing commercial confidentiality.

The group has now filed a complaint under the Aarhus Convention, a treaty signed by the EU and all its member states that guarantees public access to environmental information. The complaint is before the convention’s compliance committee, which meets four times a year.

Lighthouse Reports says the Netherlands discloses more than most other EU countries, where reporters met what they called a “wall of silence”.

item.title: Two more suspects arrested in Overasselt shooting inquiry
item.description:
Two more suspects arrested in Overasselt shooting inquiry

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two men have been arrested in Amsterdam during the investigation into a fatal shooting at a farmhouse in Gelderland.

Police said they had also recovered guns, including an automatic weapon, during searches of houses in the capital, Diemen and Hoofddorp on Tuesday.

A group of armed men descended on the small village of Overasselt in the early hours of September 1 and opened fire on a farmhouse, killing a security guard and injuring two police officers.

The man living in the house, 28-year-old Jan G., was arrested in Germany two weeks ago on suspicion of trying to smuggle cocaine through the port of Dunkirk.

He is believed to have been targeted as retribution for a stolen drugs shipment, according to a video that police obtained in the days afterwards.

Bolle Jos

The Telegraaf reported that the 1,283kg shipment belonged to “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, Europe’s most wanted criminal, who is believed to be living in Sierra Leone.

The arrest of the two suspects, aged 24 and 25, takes the total number of arrests to 36. Most of the others have appeared in court charged with murder or manslaughter.

Two of the suspects are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

A third man, aged 19, was arrested at one of the houses raided by police. His connection to the gang is being investigated.

item.title: Education cuts loom if talks with unions on welfare reforms fail
item.description:
Education cuts loom if talks with unions on welfare reforms fail

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The education budget could be cut by €1.2 billion if talks to reform social security fail to deliver enough savings, according to documents seen by NOS.

The coalition parties have agreed to scrap €6.5 billion of welfare cuts in order to get the support they need from the opposition for next year’s budget.

Some of the gap has been plugged by raising more from savers and investors, but the cabinet expects to be left with a €3 billion shortfall.

Prime minister Rob Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen are due to meet trade unions to discuss cost-saving reforms to the long-term sickness benefit WIA. “If the savings are less than we expect, the cabinet will identify additional measures,” Jetten said.

As a last resort the government could save €1.2 billion by not raising the education department’s budget in line with inflation, which would force it to make savings.

The move would be unpopular with Jetten’s own party D66, which campaigned to reverse the previous cabinet’s €2 billion cuts package and sees higher education as one of its flagship policy areas.

NOS reported that the prospect of having to make cuts in education was intended to put pressure on D66’s base to demand concessions from trade unions on social security.

Parliament is due to begin a two-day debate on the detailed budget plans on Wednesday.

item.title: Rail union demands action on violence against train staff
item.description:
Rail union demands action on violence against train staff

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Violence against train staff is getting out of control, rail union VVMC has said in a call to politicians. The union says conductors and other employees of national rail company NS are increasingly being assaulted, threatened, and spat at by passengers.

In a letter reported by NOS, the union cites NS figures showing that reports of aggression and violence against staff more than doubled from 2,672 in 2023 to 6,442 in 2025. According to those figures, there have been 5,088 reports so far this year, including 1,368 involving physical violence and 105 threats with a weapon.

“These are no longer unpleasant situations,” the union wrote, according to NOS. “These are serious incidents of violence against people carrying out their public duty.”

The letter lists several recent attacks. In February, a conductor at Rotterdam Blaak station was beaten unconscious. The same happened to a conductor at Den Dolder station 6 months later.

On August 6, several NS staff and police officers were injured during the arrest of an aggressive passenger at Almere Centrum station. According to the union, one NS employee lost part of his thumb after being bitten, and a colleague suffered a broken wrist and torn tendons.

Lost powers
The union also complained that senior conductors lost their enforcement powers in 2022. Since then, they can no longer write up offenders themselves or check personal details in the national population register.

Senior conductors were given bodycams this year, but the union says that does not make up for the powers they lost.

A VVMC spokesperson told news agency ANP that the union wants more NS security and service staff on trains.

“Politicians can no longer make do with stating that aggression is unacceptable. Action is needed now,” the letter says, according to NOS.

Licence register
The letter follows the cabinet’s announcement on Tuesday that public transport enforcement officers will get access to the driving licence register. From Thursday, employers can apply to vehicle authority RDW for access.

Officers will then be able to use licence photos to identify fare dodgers and troublemakers who carry no ID, instead of waiting for the police.

item.title: Peak birthday season: more NL celebrations today than any other
item.description:
Peak birthday season: more NL celebrations today than any other

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More people in the Netherlands are celebrating their birthday on Wednesday than on any other day of the year, with some 44,000 sharing September 30, according to national statistics office CBS.

On average, 41,000 people in the Netherlands have a birthday every day. The number peaks in late September and early May.

The figures are taken from over 15 million people who were born in the country and whose birth is officially registered with a local council. Those born abroad are not included.

Apart from leap day, New Year’s Day is the least common birthday. Christmas, Sinterklaas, and Liberation Day also have relatively few. The CBS said this may be because planned births, such as caesarean sections, are less often scheduled on holidays.

Birth patterns have also shifted over time. People born between 1940 and 1980 were more often born in spring, while summer and late-summer birthdays are more common among those born since 1980.

The CBS said the arrival of the contraceptive pill in the 1960s, which made pregnancies easier to plan, may explain the change.

item.title: Hundreds of thousands more to pay tax on savings, NOS says
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands more to pay tax on savings, NOS says

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Hundreds of thousands more people in the Netherlands are set to pay tax on their savings and investments from 2028 under a revised plan for box 3, the tax on wealth, according to leaked details of the cabinet’s deliberations with opposition parties.

Box 3 covers savings, shares, crypto and second homes, and around 2.5 million people currently pay it, according to broadcaster NOS. At present the tax rate is 36% on an assumed return on those assets, with a tax-free allowance of €59,357 per person.

Under a new law on box 3 rules approved by MPs in February, people were to pay tax on unrealised returns on most assets every year, meaning they would pay tax on increased asset values regardless of whether they have sold the assets and made any money.

This plan is set to be dropped for shares, according to NOS, and people will only pay tax on gains from shares once they sell them. This was a demand by right-wing parties such as far-right JA21.

Initially, the new system was to allow a tax-free return of €1,800 per person a year. That has reportedly been cut to €1,000, helping offset the losses anticipated by moving to a realised gains system.

Businesses affected 

People who run their own private limited company (bv) will also be affected. The amount they can borrow from their own company on favourable tax terms is set to fall from €500,000 to €100,000. The rules on borrowing from a company to buy a home will stay the same.

At the same time, tax on profits that owners pay out to themselves will be cut for 4 years. The aim is to encourage them to take money out of the company, which would bring in extra tax revenue in the short term.

The measures are expected to raise almost €500 million more than needed. The cabinet wants to use that to cut income tax, but has not yet said how.

Welfare cuts dropped

The leaked plans also confirm that planned cuts to social security are off the table, as left-wing Pro and pan-European party Volt said this week. Hans Spekman, chairman of the country’s largest trade union FNV, said on Monday evening that the unions would return to talks with the cabinet if the cuts were scrapped. Political sources told NOS that could happen as soon as next week.

JA21 said part of the funding for the box 3 changes was “unacceptable” because it hits small investors. Jan Struijs, parliamentary leader of pensioners’ party 50PLUS, said he wanted a “stress test” to show what the plans would mean for police officers, nurses and pensioners.

Finance minister Eelco Heinenis expected to set out the details in a letter to parliament ahead of this week’s budget debate. The minority cabinet needs opposition votes to get its budget through both houses of parliament.

item.title: Netherlands “blocked” Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela
item.description:
Netherlands “blocked” Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela

September 29, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government has been accused of blocking the return of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado after two flights to Curaçao and Aruba were cancelled on the same day.

Both flights were cancelled at short notice last Tuesday because of administrative “technicalities” that arose after Machado had booked to travel from her current home in Panama, according to a Spanish journalist who was embedded with her to document the trip.

The Nobel peace prize winner had hoped to slip into Venezuela via the Caribbean islands while the country’s interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, was in New York for the United Nations general assembly last week.

Officially the Netherlands supports Machado’s return so that free democratic elections can be held, something that has not happened since former president Nicolas Maduro was captured by US forces in January and replaced by Rodriguez, who was vice-president in Maduro’s regime.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said at his weekly press conference on Friday: “If Venezuela is serious about working towards a future where relations with the Netherlands and Europe are normalised, one of our conditions is that progress is made towards free and fair elections.

“Those elections are only possible if opposition leaders can participate in them.”

Trump oil deal

But behind the scenes, the Trump administration appears to be concerned that Machado’s return could destabilise the interim regime, which has struck a deal with Washington giving the US control of 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves.

Leiden university professor Wouter Veenendaal, who specialises in relations between the nations in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, told Dutch News: “I can’t prove it, but it sounds to me like The Hague has been put under pressure by the Americans.

“Although the Americans formally take a positive view of Machado, her arrival is seen as potentially threatening the relative stability that they’ve been able to create with the interim president.”

Machado has made seven attempts to reach Venezuela by land, sea and air in recent months, including twice from Curaçao and once from Aruba, but every time her efforts have been thwarted by administrative or technical problems.

Last Tuesday a ferry trip from Panama City, where she is currently living, was cancelled hours before the boat was due to leave port after the operator claimed to have discovered a serious defect with the engine.

Paperwork problem

David Alandete, a journalist with the Spanish newspaper ABC who was invited to travel with Machado, said it was clear that the Dutch government, which controls the Caribbean islands’ foreign policy, “had a hand in preventing Machado from reaching Aruba, Curaçao or Bonaire”.

“This was not simply a paperwork problem. A European government was part of the chain of decisions that kept her from moving closer to Venezuela,” he wrote on social media site X.

Is María Corina Machado a prisoner in Panama? Why has the Nobel Peace Prize winner been prevented from returning to her own country seven times? I have the facts firsthand from Panama. I was with her team this weekend and witnessed the latest attempts—and the refusals. The full… pic.twitter.com/Jk4iBuop3m

— David Alandete (@alandete) September 23, 2026

“Clearly there is something that is preventing Maria Corina Machado from returning,” Alandete said. “She has tried to enter and she’s been unable to do it.”

Jetten would neither confirm nor deny at his press conference whether the Netherlands was behind the decision to cancel Machado’s flights.

“It’s not in the interests of the co-operation we have with the [Venezuelan] opposition and the responsibility we feel for its members to say any more about it,” he said.

Caribbean journalists who asked Eric van der Burg, junior minister for kingdom relations, about the episode last week were redirected to the foreign affairs ministry in The Hague. “I can say extremely little about it,” he said, according to the Antilliaans Dagblad.

Jetten also hinted that he had been unable to persuade Rodriguez to guarantee Machado’s safe return to her country when he spoke to the interim president at the UN last week.

“It’s important that Machado and others are able to travel freely to Venezuela, and that’s why I brought it to the interim president’s attention.”

Veenendaal said the episode was typical of the way the Dutch govern Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, which are semi-autonomous nations within the kingdom, and the “democratic deficit” in their administration.

Colonial history

The islands are represented by Van der Burg at the cabinet table in The Hague, but have no say in which issues are raised. Their parliaments have no powers to question cabinet ministers about foreign policy or defence.

“A lot of decisions are taken over their heads, which is a sensitive point given the colonial history,” Veenendaal said.

“In the past the Americans have exerted a lot of pressure on The Hague behind the scenes, for example to prevent the islands becoming independent, but also because they have air bases on the islands so that they can keep an eye on Venezuela.”

“I can see Jetten’s government thinking: ‘choose your battles’. Let the Americans get their way here so that the Americans give them an easier ride on other issues such as the International Criminal Court or Ukraine.”

item.title: Five arrested after luggage left unattended at railway stations
item.description:
Five arrested after luggage left unattended at railway stations

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Five people have been arrested after four railway stations had to be partly evacuated on Tuesday morning when luggage was left unattended.

Haarlem station and surrounding buildings were closed and cleared after two stray bags were reported at around 10.15am. Some trains were unable to stop at the station.

Luggage was also left standing in Rotterdam, Utrecht and Dordrecht. Police said there was no evidence that the incidents were linked, but they described the situation as “highly unusual”.

Three people were arrested at Haarlem station, while two others were detained at Utrecht Centraal after camera footage showed them acting suspiciously just before they dumped the bags.

In Rotterdam a pedestrian tunnel was evacuated while police checked two abandoned suitcases for possible explosives.

A woman in Rotterdam later came forward to say she had left the bags while she went into the city centre. She was not arrested.

Spokesman Jan Martijn Stout told NOS the incidents appeared to be unconnected, but the suspects were be questioned about why they had left the bags behind.

“Their role is being investigated because it was a significant disruption to public order,” he said.
